newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean workers block arrests of leaders.
newsitem.headline: South Korean workers block arrests of leaders.

text.p: Militant South Korean workers wielding iron bars turned away police trying to arrest strike leaders huddled for protection on the icy grounds of a Seoul cathedral on Saturday.

In angry face-offs during the night outside Myongdong cathedral, workers rebuffed repeated attempts by plainclothes officers to serve arrest warrants on seven leaders of the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions.
They clanged their bars on iron railings to summon reinforcements each time police approached the gothic cathedral in a busy shopping district.
Confederation president Kwon Young-kil and his six deputies remained out of sight under a makeshift tent of sagging plastic sheeting pitched beneath a statue of the Virgin Mary.

Worker opposition to a new labour law that has sparked two weeks of wildcat strikes was galvanised on Friday by a Hyundai worker who staggered past ranks of riot police with his clothes on fire during a protest in the southeast city of Ulsan.
Police said Chung Jae-sung was injured after an unexploded tear gas shell ignited.
Union officials said he set fire to himself in an attempted suicide protest against the new labour law, which allows worker layoffs, shattering near-total job security.
The worker was recovering in a Seoul hospital on Saturday.
Hyundai Motors on Friday shut down its car plant in what unions described as a lockout. Workers had been turning up to the plant each day but had crippled production by working only intermittently.
The controversial new labour law, rammed through parliament by the ruling party, allows employers to lay off workers, set flexible work hours and use part-time labour.
International pressure on the South Korean government over the law, and its handling of the strikes mounted.
OECD chief Donald Johnston said he was worried about the turmoil and had reminded Seoul's envoy in Paris of the organisation's commitment to human rights.

South Korea became the 29th member of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development in December, and the OECD said Johnston used his first meeting with the new Korean envoy to express concern and dismay among its members.
The OECD would review the law on January 22, a statement by the free-market organisation said.
OECD members had previously protested against the imrisonment in Korea of union leaders.

"The Korean government undertook to reform its legislation in line with internationally accepted standards, including such basic rights as freedom of association and collective bargaining," the statement added.

The head of the International Labour Organisation wrote to South Korean President Kim Young-sam after a global trade union group asked him to intervene to prevent Seoul arresting strike leaders, an ILO spokesman said.

The International Confederation of Free Trade Unions (ICFTU) on Thursday expressed concern about possible imminent arrests. ICFTU leaders were due in Seoul on Saturday to try to persuade President Kim do dump the bill.
ILO spokesman Michel Barton said freedom of trade unions was a fundamental principle of the United Nations agency, which promotes basic workers' rights in its 174 member states.

South Korea, which joined the ILO in 1991, has twice been reprimanded by an ILO committee for arrests of trade unionists and non-recognition of trade unions in violation of ILO principles of freedom of association.
A South Korean court issued the arrest warrants on Friday even though union leaders have threatened nationwide stoppages, including a public sector shutdown, if they are seized.
State prosecutors asked for the warrants on charges of obstructing business by staging illegal strikes.
